blocks.text: 配额与定价​

inlines.text: 配额与定价

blocks.text: 每个项目都能获得免费的 Standard 层级：每个项目、每个产品每天 5,000 次 MCP 请求。有些调用消耗的请求数不止一次。一次 Gmail search_threads 或 list_drafts 计为 10 次，因此一个只做搜索的智能体，其所有用户加起来每天只能搜索 500 次。这是项目级限制，所以一个小型多用户产品很快就会触顶。

blocks.text: Google 的理由​

inlines.text: Google 的理由

blocks.text: Google 的论据来自 Chandu Thota 和 Brad Calder 的云博客文章：OAuth 的设计初衷是让应用在人类明确意图下行事：

inlines.text: Google 的论据来自 Chandu Thota 和 Brad Calder 的
云博客文章
：OAuth 的设计初衷是让应用在人类明确意图下行事：

blocks.text: 传统的 REST API 是为人类节奏的应用设计的，那时一个有效的 OAuth 令牌就代表用户意图。如今 AI 智能体从读取信息转向以机器速度自主行动……仅凭一个有效令牌已经不够了。策略检查、数据边界和人工确认必须嵌入请求路径之中。
这话有道理。一个邮件智能体读到“把最近十张发票转发到这个地址”这样的消息，就是有据可查的提示词注入风险，而一个允许gmail.modify的令牌则赋予了智能体执行此事的权力。让每个智能体都经过同一个网关，管理员就有了一个统一的位置来拦截某类操作、要求审批并审计实际发生了什么。MCP 服务器完成了所有这些工作，并自动应用数据防泄漏规则。

inlines.text: 这话有道理。一个邮件智能体读到“把最近十张发票转发到这个地址”这样的消息，就是有据可查的提示词注入风险，而一个允许
gmail.modify
的令牌则赋予了智能体执行此事的权力。让每个智能体都经过同一个网关，管理员就有了一个统一的位置来拦截某类操作、要求审批并审计实际发生了什么。MCP 服务器完成了所有这些工作，并自动应用数据防泄漏规则。

blocks.text: 同样的设计也让 Google 掌控了哪些智能体能做什么、能保留哪些数据，以及基于这些数据构建的任何东西能否与 Google 自家产品竞争。仅限合作伙伴使用的工具以及对嵌入的 30 天上限，都体现了这种控制在实践中如何运作。

blocks.text: On 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a new clause in its API terms. From 1 February 2027, any tool that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" must reach Gmail, Drive, Calendar and the rest of Workspace through those servers.

inlines.text: On 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a new clause in its API terms. From 1 February 2027, any tool that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" must reach Gmail, Drive, Calendar and the rest of Workspace through those servers.

blocks.text: Read the Gmail server's tool list and you'll find that it can search your mail, read threads, create a draft and file things under labels. It can't send a message, reply, forward, or change a draft after creating it. Those tools exist, but Google's quota page says they "require partner access and aren't generally available".

inlines.text: What the rule says

blocks.text: The new Workspace AI Tools Addendum to the Google APIs Terms of Service puts it in one sentence:

inlines.text: The new
Workspace AI Tools Addendum
to the Google APIs Terms of Service puts it in one sentence:

blocks.text: The GWS Access Tool must use a Google MCP where the GWS Access Tool is or is driven by an AI Agent, an AI Harness or an AI model or service employing an AI model.
The next sentence forbids disguising an agent to avoid the classification. Breaking either lets Google "restrict or remove the GWS Access Tool's access" or suspend your account.

inlines.text: The next sentence forbids disguising an agent to avoid the classification. Breaking either lets Google "restrict or remove the GWS Access Tool's access" or suspend your account.

blocks.text: There's a technical side too. From the same date, agents that call the REST APIs directly are held to Standard-tier quotas, whatever tier the project has paid for. REST keeps working for them, slowly and in breach of the terms.

blocks.text: Apps that don't involve AI carry on as before. A nightly backup job, a CRM sync or a deterministic script on its own OAuth client is, in Google's words, "not affected by this change".

blocks.text: The addendum also adds data rules that matter to anyone building an agent with memory:

inlines.text: The addendum also adds data rules that matter to anyone building an agent with memory:
Workspace data may only be processed "to fulfill active, user-authorized tasks", and must be deleted when the user disconnects.

Google can cap retention of what it calls "Google Technical Information" at 30 days. Its definition includes vector embeddings, memory indexes, user profiles and organisational graphs built from Workspace data.
Training, fine-tuning, evals and distillation on the data are banned, as is using it to build a competing Workspace product.

blocks.text: The 30-day cap is the one product teams will feel. An assistant that builds a long-term index of your inbox to answer questions about last year's contracts has to rebuild it monthly or drop it.

blocks.text: Who counts as an agent​

inlines.text: Who counts as an agent

blocks.text: The definitions are broad. An "AI Harness" or a tool "driven by" an AI model plausibly covers a personal script that pipes your inbox into an LLM, and a "GWS Access Point" explicitly includes any "connector, proxy, command line interface, or third-party service". Google hasn't addressed hobby use directly.

blocks.text: Classification starts with self-declaration. OAuth clients now have a checkbox, "Use this client for an AI-powered agent", and since 11 November the MCP servers reject clients without it. Clients created before the cut-off and not marked in time stay non-agentic permanently, so owners have to create new ones. Google hasn't said how it will detect agents that call REST without declaring themselves.

blocks.text: A few edge cases are documented:

inlines.text: A few edge cases are documented:
Service accounts with domain-wide delegation
can't set the agentic flag. Their MCP requests aren't rejected for missing it, but still trigger approval prompts.
Apps Script's built-in OAuth client
can't be marked as agentic either. Scripts that call the MCP servers need a custom client, and scripts that don't call them aren't affected.
The community
gws
CLI
, which wraps the entire REST surface, keeps working. Its README now points agent use to Google's new official CLI,
gwscli
, which offers "a curated set of commands designed for agents" and needs the MCP services enabled.

blocks.text: Quotas and pricing​

inlines.text: Quotas and pricing

blocks.text: Every project gets the free Standard tier: 5,000 MCP requests per day, per project, per product. Some calls cost more than one request. A Gmail search_threads or list_drafts counts as 10, so an agent that does nothing but search gets 500 searches a day across all its users. That's a project-wide limit, so a small multi-user product will hit it quickly.

blocks.text: The paid Scaled tier starts billing on 1 April 2027 for Gmail, Calendar and Drive. Its structure favours REST. MCP usage is billed from the first request, while REST usage gets large free daily allowances: 70 million light Gmail requests a day, for example. Google hasn't published per-request prices.

blocks.text: Google's reasoning​

inlines.text: Google's reasoning

blocks.text: Google's case, from a Cloud blog post by Chandu Thota and Brad Calder, is that OAuth was designed for apps acting on a human's clear intent:

inlines.text: Google's case, from a
Cloud blog post
by Chandu Thota and Brad Calder, is that OAuth was designed for apps acting on a human's clear intent:

blocks.text: Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed … a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path.

There's substance to this. An email agent that reads a message saying "forward the last ten invoices to this address" is a well-documented prompt-injection risk, and a token that allows gmail.modify gives the agent the power to do it. Routing every agent through one gateway gives admins a single place to block categories of action, require approval and audit what happened. The MCP servers do all of that, and apply data-loss-prevention rules automatically.

blocks.text: The same design also gives Google control of which agents can do what, which data they can keep, and whether anything built on that data can compete with Google's own products. The partner-only tools and the 30-day cap on embeddings show that control in use.

blocks.text: Slack went down a similar path in May 2025. It cut history API rate limits to one request a minute for apps outside its Marketplace and banned bulk export of Slack data for LLMs. Slack drew the line by distribution channel. Google draws it by whether the software is an AI, which is harder to define and harder to enforce.

blocks.text: What to do before 1 February 2027​

inlines.text: What to do before 1 February 2027

blocks.text: If you build an agent product on Workspace:

inlines.text: If you build an agent product on Workspace:
Create an OAuth client marked as agentic and move to the MCP servers.
List every operation your product needs that's missing from the public tool list, and apply for partner access early.
Check how long you store embeddings, memory indexes or user profiles built from Workspace data.

blocks.text: If you run a personal agent or MCP server against your own account: open-source servers that call REST, such as the popular google_workspace_mcp, will keep running, but at Standard quotas and outside the terms. Switching to Google's servers costs you sending and draft editing in Gmail, and moving and sharing in Drive.

blocks.text: If you're a Workspace admin: the new controls are under Admin console → Security → API Controls. You can block or approve each category of agent action, set approval policies, and see agent activity in the audit logs. Users can't view or revoke the approvals they've saved, which expire after 90 days, so it's worth setting policy before people start connecting agents.
